title: 2026-09-04 Justice Committee
machineSummary: Heather Gardiner of Pirirakau Tribal Authority said a bill banning gang funding threatens initiatives like Kahukura and Butterbean Motivation, risking $5,000 fines. Max Marshall said funding gangs is unethical. Andrew Riddle said the bill lacks justification and violates rights.

chunks.text: Koutou, nga mema Paremata e hika ana i te kaupapa nei, tena koutou. Ko au te Kaihautu o Pirirakau Tribal Authority. I'm Heather Gardiner. As mentioned, the Kaihautu for Pirirakau Tribal Authority. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse and Care published a case study called Cauldron of Violence, Hokio Beach School and Kohitere Boys Training Center.

Its subtitle is A Case Study of the State's Role in Creating Gangs and Criminals. That's not my characterization, that's the Royal Commission's. The state took Maori children from their whanau, placed them in institutions, and subjected them to physical, sexual, and psychological abuse. Those institutions became incubators for gang formation. Children who entered without criminal affiliations emerged with them. The abuse inflicted inside those walls created the trauma, the disconnection, and the institutional loyalty that became the foundation of

gang culture in this country. The Royal Commission confirmed at least 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019. 200,000, with Maori disproportionately affected. The Prime Minister formally apologized in November 2024. He said, "You have been heard, and you are believed." The Prime Minister's chief science advisor concluded that for some people, given the structural forces at play, gang membership was inevitable from the outset.

Inevitable from the outset, yet here we are with this legislation. This bill legislates to prohibit funding to the organizations attempting to repair the damage the Crown inflicted. The Crown acknowledges it created gangs, it apologizes, and then it closes the door it opened.

77% of known gang members in Aotearoa are Maori. Maori are only 17.8% of the population. When the government introduced its gang patch and non-association laws, 83% of the people charged in the first three months were Maori. The bill targets organizations associated to gangs, but associated to is not defined.

Its reach extends to every hapu, every iwi, every marae in the country because every hapu in Aotearoa has whanau who are gang connected in some way. Under this bill, every Maori organization in the country will need to prove it has no connection to gangs in order to receive public funding.

Given that 77% of gang members are Maori and membership is intergenerational, this is asking Maori organizations to exile parts of their own whanau in order to access funds. That's structural discrimination. The government calls funding gang-associated organizations unconscionable.

The evidence says otherwise. Kahukura was a marae-based methamphetamine rehabilitation program operated by hard-to-reach with Mongrel Mob connections. It delivered nine intakes working with approximately 80 addicts. Participants reported that being among their gang whanau was a vital component in their recovery.

The program was canceled under the current government for political reasons, not for program failure. The government of the day was more interested in optics than in results. The Hurihanga initiative supports pro-social leadership from within Mongrel Mob and Black Power whanau in Porirua and Wellington.

It has a three-year independent developmental evaluation documenting its impact. Why would the government discourage this kind of positive leadership from gangs? Senior members of the Mongrel Mob Notorious chapter approached the Salvation Army to build a partnership to combat methamphetamine addiction. That is gang leadership seeking solutions, not perpetuating harm. I ask again, why would the government discourage this kind of positive leadership from within the gangs?

David Luiteli, son of a Mongrel Mob president, built Butterbean Motivation, which delivers free fitness programs, food distribution, and employment. An organization like his could be denied Crown funding because of his whakapapa, or as this bill puts it, associated to gangs.

This bill removes tools that work and replaces them with nothing. Survivors of state abuse do not navigate complex legal claims alone. They rely on grassroots Maori advocacy organization, community trusts, and Whanau Ora navigators. Many of those organizations operate in communities where gang connections exist because those are the communities where state abuse survivors live.

If those providers risk a 12-month prison sentence for passing Crown-derived funds to someone with a gang connection, they'll stop taking on gang-affiliated clients, the survivors who most need representation. State abuse created their gang connections, and they will now be abandoned by the only services capable of reaching them.

The Royal Commission recommended collective community-based healing initiatives. This bill prohibits funding to those programs if anyone involved is deemed a gang associate. The New Zealand Law Society has warned this committee that the bill contains no financial threshold. Every dollar must be tracked to the final receipt. A $200 catering invoice to a Maori-owned business could trigger a criminal investigation if a contract worker has a gang link, or a $50 petrol reimbursement to a marae volunteer with a patched uncle technically falls within scope.

That's ridiculous. The criminal pene- penalties are real, up to 12 months imprisonment, $5,000 fine. Risk-averse public servants will interpret the prohibition broadly, potentially defunding legitimate services to avoid the possibility of personal criminal liability.

The practical effect is the wholesale defunding of Māori community organizations that work in the spaces where gangs exist. The state created gangs, the Royal Commission proved it, the Prime Minister apologized for it, and now the state proposes to cut off the only funding pathways that work within gang-connected communities to address the harm the state caused.

Piri Rako asks this committee to withdraw the bill. If the committee will not do that, our written submission sets out the minimum amendments required. But to be clear, no amount of amendment fixes a bill that has a premise that the state can create a problem, apologize for creating it, and then criminalize the communities trying to solve it.

The stinks of a decision made for political convenience. Every hapū in this country should be concerned. Hmm Not because they support criminal activity, but because this bill's breadth makes every Māori community organization vulnerable to defunding based on whakapapa connections to their own people, and we find that unacceptable.

Happy to take questions. Thanks, Heta. We've got a couple of questions. Going to need to get through them in the next two minutes. We'll start with Dan Rosewarne. Yeah. Hey. Thanks, Heta. Your point around subcontracting is a good one, and I'll be asking officials to walk the committee through how this bill, as drafted, would operate in a typical Crown-funded roading project, for example.

Especially if it's involving multiple tiers of contractors and subbies. Especially if a Māori-owned subcontractor is employing another worker with gang affiliations. So, thanks for that. I was just wondering, is there any kind of examples, like roading examples, that you are aware of right now where this bill might affect them?

A specific roading example where... I mean, not off the top of my head, no. But I guess the point that I was making is that whether they be Māori organizations, Whānau Ora organizations, any organizations, there is an arms reach connection somehow to a gang member. The main example I gave in my submission is David Letele.

The Butter Bean has been supremely successful. It is highly regarded in South Auckland, and his father is a Mongrel Mob president. That seems to me could easily be interpreted as a gang associate, and therefore programs like his who have had government funding, and been very successful with that, would no longer be eligible. At the very least, it can be interpreted that way even if that's not the intent, and that's a problem.

And a question from Rima Nakley. Kia ora, Heta. Look, thank you very much. As you may know, I'm the sponsor of the bill. Thank you for your detailed submission. I first want to start off by saying, for me, personally, I'm always keeping the survivors of state abuse care and church care in my prayers.

I hear you when it comes to that word associated, and when this was pulled out of the ballot, I actually sat down on Zoom with someone that he deals with a lot of gang members, and we spoke about his concern with the word associated. So, that's something that I'm going to be working on.

So I won't address those ones, but I want you to rest assured I'm going to work on that. Second, because we're running out of time, I just want to ask you a few questions, please. And please just understand my intention. We've only got time for one question. Okay. So do you accept that Kahukura is a program initiated by Hard2Reach, and Hard2Reach is a consulting firm basically run by a Mongrel Mob member?

You accept that? Yes. And the second quick question is, do you accept that the Mongrel Mob currently engage in criminal activity? Absolutely, but they're two mutually exclusive lanes. Connecting the two and coming to the broad assumption is therefore it should be shut down, I don't agree with that.

Heta, I promise you, I'm happy to have a Zoom phone call later on. Feel free to email me, and I'll get my EA to do it up. But to me, it's not about cutting off people from having rehabilitation. It's about who's conducting the rehabilitation. That's what it is. Fantastic. Thank you very much, Heta.

Really appreciate you joining us this afternoon. Okay. And thank you for your recent submission as well. Now come to our next submitter, which is going to be Max Marshall. He's coming across in person. Thank you, Max.

Over to you. Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Hi there. Good morning, everyone. Tena koutou katoa. Thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak this afternoon. The argument that I'm putting forward is about outcome. The outcome of gangs is that they are behind drugs and criminality.

Until gangs can offer me an outcome which is different, I don't believe that we should help them. If I looked at 2026, I see mayhem, crime, human misery associated with this group. The assessment of a group is not determined by the presence of good people. For the same reason, we have a prohibition on the investment of super funds into unethical businesses and companies.

This is not a judgment on whether there are good people in the companies. Instead, our decision is based on outcome We may have had an individual who's left the group, the gang, and started their own florist business. Doesn't follow that the gang has changed.

To put it more simply, I would not want to give money to a company which was unethical, and I'd want to apply the same principle to gangs when making decisions about the distribution of public funds. And I'm happy to answer questions on my submission, either what I've said here or in my written submission.

Thank you, Max. We've got a question from Rima Naklay. Hi, Max. Thank you very much again for your inputs. And look, I hear what you were just saying. I just want to turn to your written submission. On the second page- Mm-hmm... the third last point, you wrote, "I do not believe that a government winning the elections give it a mandate to do anything,"

et cetera. And I argue this is bad law. I just want to confirm- Mm... that this was a bill that was pulled out of a ballot. So it was- Oh, yeah... what some people would say pure luck. Pure luck, yeah. Even though I don't believe in luck. But, so it wasn't something we did purposely, it was pulled out of a ballot. And, for me, it's something that's important that we don't give money to people that are selling drugs.
Yeah. I'd like to respond to that. Yes. I've spoken to expats living in Australia, and one of my friends works in construction, and she has contact with a lot of Kiwis. And part of the

reason for them moving hasn't been economic, which is the common view that's often given as to why people go over. Rosalie Bard did a study on this as part of her thesis. She's a Canterbury lecturer. And I said part of their reason for moving out was because of the law and order issue and anger and things like that. Yeah.
Thanks for that, Max. Thanks, Max. Really appreciate you joining us this afternoon. Thank you. Is Andrew online? Right.

Hi, Andrew. Thank you very much for joining us this afternoon. We've got you down for five minutes. We've read your written submission, and just leave some time at the end for questions, please. Yeah. Okay. Good afternoon. My contention is that this bill, there's no case made out to justify this piece of legislation over the status quo.

Some sort of moral outrage is just simply not enough. Needs to be more than that. I'm especially concerned that this legislation will actually prevent opportunities for moves to rehabilitate gang members and to support them through, say for example, a pandemic or all sorts of public health issues and all those sort of types of activities, to support them, gang members or gangs, when there's some sort of civil emergency, and they provide help, which has happened.

And I think there's a really stark contrast in this bill to Rob Muldoon meeting gang members in a pub and then taking some positive action to help them. This is just an exercise in vindictiveness. Full stop. Thanks, Andrew. Okay, we've got a question from Todd Stevenson.

Oh, hi, Andrew. Thanks for your submission. Just looking at your written submission, you said it's contrary to human rights under the New Zealand Bill of Rights and also the International Declaration of Human Rights. Can you be a bit more specific what New Zealand Bill of Rights breaches do you think this bill actually breaches? The first one is that it's actually punishing people without a trial.

The second one is it's discriminatory without justification. Okay. That's interesting interpretation. Thank you. Lawrence Sunam. And by the way, Todd, I'm missing your press releases. I always enjoyed your press releases. Thanks, Andrew. We'll just- Oh, thank you... we'll stay on the topic we're here to discuss. Lawrence.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you so much for your submission, Andrew. I guess two quick questions, and one of them is, although it's not covered by this one, why did you include Disney's church as a part of it? And my second question is, you mentioned around rehabilitation, and I think one of the questions we have is sort of, what is the scope that we are looking at?

Do you see it as a direct transaction with gangs, or do you see any sort of knock-on effect where public service would, in some ways, interact with gangs? You mentioned kind of emergency services, that being one of them. I just want to kind of get a sense of where do you think the scope could have been.

I think that answering your second one, when legislation talks about the Crown must not pay money directly or indirectly to a gang, and where it says that in the offenses Either to or for the benefit of an entity, knowing that entity is a gang. I think there's just so much imprecision in those two terms as to exactly who's covered, when are they covered, and there's no consideration about whether that money in question is actually for a public benefit or what. Or whether it's for a payment for

some sort of work-related service like that was referred to by the person sitting to your right about roading. Thanks, Andrew. And we've got a- The Destiny Church one is, I just think that Destiny Church is equivalent of a gang in the way it behaves. Thank you. Thank you. And we've got a question from Rima Naqvi.

Hi, Mr. Riddle. Can I ask you, if I was to trick you into taking poison, and then I was to get you to pay for the antidote, do you have a right to be morally outraged or not? I think my outrage is actually that the person who's promoting the bill is actually on a select committee- So you don't have an answer to that... equivalent of being a judge and jury.

Okay. That committee's point is to actually hear a case, not- Right. So you want us to give money to people- Rima... somebody a platform to argue for their own legislation. I'm outraged about that. I think that this is sort of symptomatic of a bloody government which has no concept of proper- Go say that to the mother- Rima... who has the children that are addicted to meth.

Excuse me. Okay. Thank you very much, Andrew. Really appreciate your time this afternoon and your written submission as well. Thank you for joining us. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. I apologize. I don't. Okay. Thank you officials. That concludes our work on that today. We will pick this up again when we have our next round of submissions, and we'll pick up our feedback to you then.
